concept.technique_name: lateral surface area of a cone via slant height

examples.problem_statement: Your friend’s cap is in the shape of a right circular cone of base radius 14 cm and height 26.5 cm. The approximate area of the sheet required to make 7 such caps is

solution.result: Sheet area for one cap = lateral surface area of the cone
solution.description: Identify that the sheet forms only the curved side of the cap, so the area needed for one cap is the cone's lateral surface area \pi r l, not the total surface area.
Combine the base radius 14 and the vertical height 26.5 with the Pythagorean relation to get the slant height l, which the area formula needs.
Round the slant height to 30, the approximation the book uses since the question asks only for an approximate area.
Multiply the one-cap lateral area by 7 to cover all seven caps, substituting r = 14 and the rounded l = 30.

key_reminders: Lateral (curved) surface area of a right circular cone is \pi r l.
The slant height l comes from r^2 + h^2 = l^2; it is not the given vertical height.
Scale the single-object area by the count only after the per-object area is fixed.
common_mistakes: Using the vertical height 26.5 directly in \pi r l instead of first computing the slant height 29.97.
Computing the area of one cap and forgetting the factor of 7.
Adding the base circle area \pi r^2, which a cap does not require.

concept.technique_name: unit conversion by multiplying conversion ratios so units cancel

examples.problem_statement: Joe’s car can travel 36 miles per gallon of fuel. Approximately how many kilometers can the car travel on 10 liters of fuel? (5 miles = approximately 8 kilometers; 1 gallon = approximately 4 liters)

solution.result: miles and gallons cancel, leaving kilometers per liter
solution.description: Write the given fuel economy against the two conversion ratios, orienting each ratio so that the miles unit and the gallons unit cancel and only km per L survives.
Carry out the arithmetic of that chain of ratios to get the car's fuel economy expressed in kilometers per liter.
Apply the converted rate to the 10 liters actually in the tank, since the question asks for distance rather than a rate.

key_reminders: Orient each conversion ratio so the unwanted unit appears once on top and once on the bottom and cancels.
Convert the rate fully before multiplying by the given quantity of fuel.
common_mistakes: Inverting a ratio, e.g. multiplying by 5/8 instead of 8/5, or by 4 liters per gallon instead of 1 gallon per 4 liters.
Stopping at 14.4 and reporting the rate instead of multiplying by the 10 liters.

concept.technique_name: successive percentage change via multiplying factors

examples.problem_statement: Abhimanyu Banerjee has 72% vision in his left eye and 68% vision in his right eye. On corrective therapy, he starts wearing contact lenses, which augment his vision by 15% in the left eye and 11% in the right eye. Find out the percentage of normal vision that he possesses after corrective therapy. (Assume that a person’s eyesight is a multiplicative construct of the eyesight’s of his left and right eyes)

solution.result: the single product that represents post-therapy vision
solution.description: Set up one product: each eye contributes its current vision as a decimal and each augmentation contributes a multiplier of 1 plus the percentage increase, because the problem states eyesight is a multiplicative construct.
Evaluate the left-eye pair, applying the 15% augmentation to the 72% base vision of the left eye.
Evaluate the right-eye pair, applying the 11% augmentation to the 68% base vision of the right eye.
Multiply the two corrected eye values together to combine them into overall vision, then read the decimal as a percentage of normal vision.

key_reminders: An increase of x% is applied as a multiplier of 1 + x/100, never by adding x to a percentage base.
Successive multiplicative effects compose by multiplying their factors in any order.
common_mistakes: Adding the augmentations to the base vision (72 + 15 and 68 + 11) instead of multiplying by 1.15 and 1.11.
Averaging the two eyes instead of multiplying them, despite the stated multiplicative construct.
